flatmate.io

What I learned building an appAgentic first

Samuel Zink · Final check-in · October 2026

  • Hi everyone. Today I'll show you my journey with flatmate.io, and what I learned building an app agentic first.

Choosing a new flatmatehappens in a group chat.

Real messages · anonymised

My idea

One app for the whole flat share. Everyone sees the same applicants and votes on them. The app turns all votes into a ranking.

1Collect 2Screen 3Vote 4Invite
  • A quick recap. In big flat shares, choosing a new flatmate happens in a crowded group chat. People lose track, and one or two people do all the work.
  • These are real messages from our chat. One person doesn't know when the casting is. Others feel strange deciding for 13 people with only four of them. That doesn't feel fair.
  • My idea: one app for the whole process. Everyone sees the same applicants, everyone votes, and every vote counts.

What real users confirmed,and what is still open.

Confirmed in user tests

New users can join and vote in under 3 minutes.

I set this goal before the test. The tester reached it without help.

One clear next step works better than a dashboard.

A notification bell only distracted the tester, so I removed it.

The vote scale explains itself.

Only partly. Testers wanted to change their vote, so I added that.

Not verified yet · made-up data only

A hidden ranking motivates people to vote.

More than 80 % of a flat share really vote.

Why no real casting yet?

Applications contain personal data. First I want to close the open database security questions. Until then, I only use made-up data.

I also let AI agents test every new feature in persona tests. That finds mistakes early. But only real users can confirm or invalidate a hypothesis.

  • My first hypotheses: a new user can join with an invite link and vote within three minutes, without help. And one clear next step works better than a dashboard.
  • User tests confirmed both. The vote scale was only partly clear, so I improved it.
  • Still open: does a hidden ranking motivate people, and do more than 80 % of a flat vote? I need real casting data for that, and my database must be GDPR-safe first.
  • AI persona tests find bugs early, but only real people can confirm a hypothesis.

From F3 on · core first, then in parallel

How I started · one feature after the other

Oct 2 · core flow works
full featurecoreimprovements, several agents in parallel

“Screening Pass is merged and done for now.” me, Oct 2

  • At first I built every feature completely before the next. After three features I still couldn't show a complete flow.
  • So from F3 on, I built only the core of each feature first. Then I improved them in parallel. They touched different parts of the app, so several agents could work at the same time. On October 2 the core flow worked for the first time. I should have done this from the start.

Each feature slice gets a fresh session. The feature plan carries the living memory.

  • This is how I built each slice. My loop: agents explore the code, Opus proposes a plan, and I review the specs. A separate agent attacks the plan. Sonnet implements, Opus reviews, checks run, and I click through it myself. If I want changes, it goes back. Then code review and a Copilot review.

Detailed specs were hard to change.

What went wrong

Newer decisions contradicted older specs.
The AI misread some specs.
Outdated specs still steered the AI.

Example: changing your vote

My specs said: no changing votes, and nobody sees who voted how. I wanted to avoid social pressure. But testers wanted more control, so I changed my mind.

ClaudeBut you clearly stated in the specs that you don't want this.
MeI know. Do it anyway.

Lesson: keep early specs flexible. Many details I accepted “for now” were hard to change later.

  • Precise specs help, but rigid specs are a problem. When I changed a decision, the AI kept pointing to the old specs.
  • Testers wanted to change their vote. My specs said no, to avoid social pressure. So Claude said: "But you don't want this." And I said: "I know. Do it anyway."
  • The AI follows specs very literally. So my lesson: detailed, yes, but flexible. A new decision must beat an old spec.

Where should my tests run?

GitHub runnerUSA
Supabase databaseEU · Ireland

CI → live database

6–10 min · timeouts

CI → database inside the runner

~4 min

New problem

With features in parallel, several local test runs hit the live database at once. More timeouts.

But the live DB found

· sign-in limits of the platform
· an API path I had closed
· a bug in connection pooling

Next time

First learn what differs between live and local. Then build a fast local check around it.

  • At first, all tests ran against my live database in the EU. But GitHub's runners are in the US, so CI had timeouts.
  • So CI now uses a database inside the runner, and locally I test against the live one. That found bugs that only happen on the real platform. But with parallel features, the live database got overloaded again.
  • Next time: local by default, live only regularly.

in the codein the plan
  • In the reviews I saw the same mistakes again and again. So I wrote them into hazard files and CLAUDE.md.
  • At the end, reviews found far fewer problems, and pull requests needed fewer rounds. And the remaining mistakes moved: the code did what the plan said, so if something was wrong, it was the plan.

Knowing what mattersfor the budget I have.

Sep 22–25

My agents stopped in the middle of tasks, four times in one week. The limit was reached.

Sep 30

Half of my weekly budget was gone. I built F4 before F3, so the pitch was ready.

Oct 7

76 % used. I skipped two refactors on purpose, before I started them.

Oct 13

I wrote an idea down and postponed it.

Nothing to burn tokens on right now.
  • At the start, I sometimes ran out of tokens in the middle of the week, with half-finished features. Later I planned the whole week: which features do I start, and which do I really finish? Some ideas I just wrote down for later.

I kept AI out of my app, on purpose.

Choosing a flatmate is a decision about people. My rule from day one: AI may structure text, but it never decides about people.

But to learn, I built two AI tools anyway

1

Application parser

Built with n8n. It turns an application into form fields.

2

Search over my specs

A RAG for Claude. It finds spec information faster.

  • In the product, I kept AI out of every automatic evaluation. Under the EU AI Act, AI in areas like housing assistance counts as high-risk, and picking tenants is very close to that.
  • But to learn, I built two tools.

Tool 1: an application parser

n8n · applicant-parse · recorded run

Two paths: a text message, or a screenshot. Both end in the same form fields.

Tool 2: a spec search for Claude

My two-tier approach

Question from Claude
Tier 1 · current docsThe specs that are valid today
clear answer → done
Tier 2 · archiveOld docs, only if tier 1 has no clear answer

90 documents · 1,284 chunks · runs locally

Same result, very different cost

Haiku 5.518 / 19$0.015
Opus 5.518 / 19$0.66

Open problem

Questions the docs can't answer looked as close as real ones. A larger embedding model might help. Not tested yet.

  • Second, a search over my specs for Claude, so it finds information faster. Current docs come first, old docs only if needed. That way outdated specs are used much less. Haiku answered as well as Opus, for a fraction of the cost. One problem: some questions the docs can't answer looked as close as real ones.

Bigger flat shares

That's why it is v0.1, not v1.

  • What's next? First I finish v0.1, with a few security changes in the database.
  • Then the first real household: a friend will soon start a casting in his flat. It's a smaller flat, so it's a good first test.
  • After that, bigger flat shares, once I'm sure it's secure and I won't end up in jail. That's why it's v0.1, not v1.

Five things I'd tell myself on day one.

1

Build a thin slice first.Depth comes later.

2

Keep early specs flexible.User tests will change your mind.

3

Turn every mistake into a rule.A lint beats a memory.

4

Check your budget before you start.Postpone what can wait.

5

Only real users prove a hypothesis.AI tests find mistakes early.

A appendix

  • Five things I'd tell myself on day one:
  • Build a thin slice first.
  • Keep specs detailed, but flexible.
  • Turn every mistake into a rule.
  • Plan your budget and pick the right model.
  • And go to real users early. Only they give you real feedback.

Architecture of the process.

docs spec chain→ OpenSpec change→ plan file→ pre-mortem→ apply→ review→ gates→ PR

Hierarchy of authority · higher wins

GUARDRAILS SRD PRD Compliance UX design system
  • Full pipeline from docs to PR, and which document wins when two disagree.

The nine guardrail lints.

LintWhat it stops
import-boundaryroutes and components importing the raw database client
session-contexta session-wide SET; session context only via the one transaction helper
rls-coveragea household table without any RLS policy
data-inventorya column without a declared privacy category, purpose and retention
definer-coveragea SECURITY DEFINER function without search_path or a raw-SQL test
migration-shapemigrations that abort half-applied (enum value + other SQL, ADD without IF NOT EXISTS)
guarded-testsan invariant test that is deleted, skipped or emptied
pending-feedbacka plain submit button, or a page without a loading skeleton
role-readsan authorization check against a role instead of a stored permission
  • All nine run in npm run verify on every push. Plain TypeScript, no parser: honest about what they can't see.
